1.pericope_label: Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth a declaration

schools.summary: Chrysostom sees the writer refusing to rest on his own authority at all: so far was the Evangelist from being content with his single testimony that he refers the whole to the apostles, seeking from them a confirmation of his words, since our chief ground for believing a thing is that we derive it from those who actually saw.

Gill argues that the many cannot be the authentic historians of evangelical facts, since two men cannot with any propriety be called many, and Luke would hardly insinuate a deficiency in them. Calvin is less easy about the tone than the rest of the bench. Though Luke deals gently with those who wrote before him, he does not altogether approve their labours: he does not say they wrote of matters they were imperfectly acquainted with, but by laying claim to certainty he modestly denies their title to full and unshaken confidence. Calvin thinks they may have erred more from want of consideration than from malice, so that no fierceness of attack was called for, and that these were little more than historical sketches, harmless at the time, which if not promptly counteracted would afterwards have done serious injury to the faith.

Henry keeps the charitable reading and draws a rule from it: the labours of others in the gospel of Christ, if faithful and honest, we ought to commend and encourage rather than despise, though chargeable with many deficiencies, and their service must not be reckoned to supersede ours but rather to quicken it.

Wesley agrees in a line that Matthew and Mark are not meant and that John did not write so early. Clarke lays out what is known of the writer: Lardner took Luke for a Jew by birth, Michaelis for a Gentile, arguing from the way Paul distinguishes those of the circumcision from Lucas and Demas; some ancients and some judicious moderns make him one of the two who walked to Emmaus; and all the ancients of repute agree that he was a physician. The tradition that he was also a painter of the Virgin Clarke dismisses as fabulous, since no writer attributes the skill to him before Nicephorus in the fourteenth century.

Ellicott takes the verse as evidence that written documents professing to give the Gospel history already existed when Luke wrote, and hears no tone of disparagement at all — the writer simply feels his predecessors have not exhausted the subject and that his own inquiries enable him to add something. Robertson notes how uncommon the opening word is, occurring here alone in the New Testament though ordinary in literary Attic, and observes that the verb rendered taken in hand is the one Hippocrates and Galen use in the introductions to their medical works, common in the papyri for simply undertaking a thing; he adds that the motive is universal, every author being moved by the sense that there is still room for his book. Barnes reaches the same conclusion about the Emmaus story from the text itself, since Luke does not profess to have been an eyewitness, and reports the uniform testimony of the fathers that he was the companion of Paul and that what he set down was in effect the gospel Paul preached. On the last participle Robertson notes a real ambiguity, the word meaning fully persuaded of persons and completed of things; Ellicott renders it accomplished among us, Calvin things fully ascertained.

2.pericope_label: That thou mightest know the certainty of those things

schools.summary: Gill identifies the witnesses as the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples. Calvin takes the verb for tracing as a metaphor from those who tread in another's footsteps so that nothing may escape them, and recalls Demosthenes using it of an investigation so diligent that the man perceived all that was done as well as if he had been a spectator.

Clarke defends the reading of the word for the message as the gospel rather than the personal Word, since no inspired penman uses the term of Christ himself except John. On the writer's qualification he states a doctrine of inspiration: the gift of the Spirit was never designed to set aside the powers God has already endued the soul with, these being as truly his gifts as the Spirit is; Luke set himself by impartial inquiry to find the whole truth, and the Spirit so directed it that he was preserved from every particle of error. Wesley says Luke describes in order of time, the acts of Christ and then of the apostles, but in many smaller circumstances does not observe it.

Ellicott finds something noticeable in the candour with which the writer disclaims the character of an eyewitness, and notes that the verb rendered delivered is Paul's word for what he received concerning the Supper and the Resurrection. Robertson will not let the modern sense of tradition intrude: the handing down here was dependable, not mere wives' fables, and both written and oral sources lay open to Luke. He notes that the word for eyewitnesses means seeing with one's own eyes, occurs here only in the New Testament and belongs to the medical vocabulary, while the word for ministers means under-rowers or attendants; and he observes that from the beginning must mean the beginning of the ministry, which is why the childhood narratives go behind it, such matters not having formed part of the traditional preaching. Barnes renders the phrase about tracing as having exactly traced everything from the first, and draws two conclusions: that God does not set aside our natural faculties, since no man is convinced of the truth of religion who does not investigate; and that Luke's inspiration was consistent with using them. On the order claimed, Barnes denies exact chronology is meant at all, while Ellicott allows a distinct aim at chronological arrangement but cautions that where Luke varies from the other Gospels it does not follow that his is the true order. Robertson closes on the last word, from a verb meaning to totter with the negative prefixed: Luke promises a narrative that will not slip.

5.pericope_label: There was in the days of Herod a certain priest named Zacharias

schools.summary: Chrysostom finds a graded design in the pairing: the historian relates one marvellous event before another, the less before the greater, for since a virgin was about to become a mother it had been fore-ordained that the old should first conceive.

Calvin explains the order with an image: Luke begins with John the Baptist as a man who was going to speak about the daylight would commence with the dawn, securing our respect for him while he is yet unborn so that he might afterwards be heard with the more profound veneration. On the note of time he flatly denies the common inference. Those who argue that the sceptre departed because Herod was a foreigner do not correctly understand the patriarch's prophecy, which promises the Messiah not merely after royal authority had been taken from the Jews but after it had been removed from the tribe of Judah; the sceptre did not break because Herod was foreign, but because whatever relics of rank still lingered in that tribe were carried off by his robbery — the Sanhedrim, chosen out of the family of David, having lasted until Herod avenged an old condemnation by a shocking slaughter of the judges. Gill keeps to the plain fact that Herod held all Judea by deputation from the emperor.

Henry takes the note of time as proof that the sceptre was quite departed from Judah and that now was the moment for Shiloh to come, the family of David being sunk at the very point when it was to rise again in the Messiah; and he draws the comfort out, that none ought to despair of the reviving of religion even when civil liberties are lost: Israel enslaved, and yet then comes the glory of Israel. He adds what the choice of starting point gains, since the two preceding evangelists began with John's baptism while this one gives a fuller account of the forerunner, the morning star to the Sun of righteousness.

Clarke argues the same as Henry from Herod's descent, an Idumean who professed himself a proselyte but regarded no religion further than it served his ambition, so that for the first time the throne of Judah was filled by a man not of Jewish extraction. He also turns the dating itself into evidence: anyone alive when the Gospel was published might have applied to the families named, and in all that age no man arose to call the account in question. Wesley notes only that each course served seven days, every priest's part being assigned him by lot.

Robertson marks a seam in the Greek itself: the verb is not the ordinary word for was but one meaning there arose, and with it the literary polish of the preface disappears, so that to the end of the second chapter we have the most Hebraistic passage in Luke's writings, resting plainly on documents or notes of oral tradition. He tells the story throughout from Mary's standpoint as Matthew tells his from Joseph's. Robertson counts twenty-four courses, Abijah the eighth, each serving from sabbath to sabbath twice a year, and quotes Plummer that to be a priest and married to a priest's daughter was a double distinction. Ellicott notes a complication, that only four courses are named as returning from the Captivity and Abijah is not among them, though the name reappears in later lists; and since priests might marry outside their own caste within limits, he thinks priestly descent on both sides worth the notice, observing that Elisabeth's name in its Hebrew form had belonged to Aaron's own wife.

6.pericope_label: They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments

schools.summary: Gill fixes where the commendation is registered: not as the Pharisees, righteous only before men, but in the sight of God, and therefore not justified by the deeds of the law but made righteous through the righteousness of Christ, as the saints before his coming were as truly as those after it. Calvin insists the order between the two halves of the verse matters more than the division within either: our first study ought to be to approve ourselves to God, who chiefly requires a sincere heart, so that whoever regulates his outward life by obedience while neglecting uprightness of heart has inverted the sequence. He then raises the obvious objection against himself — that a couple blameless in keeping the law would have no need of the grace of Christ — and answers that such commendations must be taken with an exception, God dealing with his servants according to a covenant whose first clause is free reconciliation and daily pardon; their pious endeavours fall far short of perfection, so the righteousness commended rests on his forbearance in not reckoning their remaining unrighteousness. He will not accept the shorter solution that Luke means only that they were righteous by faith, calling that a torturing of the words which states a part of the truth and not the whole. On the childlessness Calvin counts two hindrances rather than one, barrenness in the prime of life and now an age which of itself shuts up the womb.

Clarke divides the praise between two lives, upright in all their outward conduct in civil affairs and before God possessing the spirit of the religion they professed — what a sacred pair, he exclaims, who made their duty to God, to their neighbour and to themselves walk constantly hand in hand. He also sets the three annunciations side by side, God foretelling Isaac's birth, the angel of the Lord John's, and Gabriel Christ's. Wesley renders the two nouns moral commandments and ceremonial ordinances and breaks off into prayer that our own obedience might be as sincere and universal.

Robertson hears an Old Testament conception in the very idiom, and borrows Ragg's phrase for the group this couple belongs to, the noblest product of Old Testament education, privileged to see with clear eyes the dawn of the New Testament revelation. Ellicott takes the first noun to cover all the moral laws of the Pentateuch and the second its outward and ceremonial rules; he prefers Wycliff's rendering of the closing clause, that they had gone far in their days.

8.pericope_label: His lot was to burn incense when he went into the temple

schools.summary: Gill is careful about the status of the lot: it was not an original settled law of God but a custom which in process of time, through the sheer number of the priests, took place and prevailed. Calvin uses the arrangement to teach mediation. The twice-daily incense was expressly enjoined by the law of God, while the courses were David's ordering, and David ordained nothing the law had not prescribed, only pointing out a plan by which each family might take its turn. The word Luke uses means the sanctuary proper, which deserves attention since it can elsewhere take in the outer court; Zacharias goes where none but priests were permitted, and the people stand at a great distance, the altar of sacrifice intervening. Whenever a priest entered the holy place he went as it were into the presence of God, to stand between him and the people; and it was the Lord's will to have this impressed on them, that no mortal is allowed access to heaven without a priest going before. The design of the incense itself was to remind believers that the sweet savour of their prayers does not ascend except through the sacrifice of that Mediator.

Clarke reports from the Talmud that the priests divided the functions of the sacerdotal office among themselves by lot, and adds the shadow across the scene: this was the temple where God used to manifest his presence, though long before this time he had forsaken it, and yet on this occasion the angel of his presence visited it again.

Ellicott explains the two layers, the order of the courses settled by rotation and the distribution of functions within the week by lot, and then disposes of an old hope built on it: attempts have been made to fix the precise date of these events, and so of the Nativity, by reckoning back from the destruction of the Temple, when the course of Joiarib is known to have been ministering on the ninth day of Ab, but all such calculations are necessarily more or less precarious. He also says why the office was the most distinctive of all priestly acts, since the incense symbolised the presenting of the people's prayers with the priest's own joined to them, so that at such a moment every hope of a man who looked for the Christ would gather itself into one great intercession. Robertson glosses the verb literally as he obtained the lot, an old word in use from Homer onward, and notes what the outcome meant: only once in a lifetime did a priest obtain the lot of entering the sanctuary and burning incense on the golden altar, the fortunate lot being a white stone. He borrows Vincent's account of the ritual — the priests ascending the steps, spreading the coals and arranging the incense, until the officiating priest was left alone to await the president's signal — and observes that this was probably the moment when the angel appeared, quoting Ragg that this was the great moment of Zacharias's life, and his heart was no doubt alert for the supernatural.

10.pericope_label: There appeared unto him an angel of the Lord

schools.summary: Chrysostom keeps both actions in one frame: Zacharias had entered the temple to offer prayers for all men, interceding between God and man, and it was there he saw an angel standing.

Augustine presses the question whose prayer was heard. It is not likely that Zacharias, offering sacrifice for the redemption of the people, would neglect the public petitions in order to pray, an old man with an old wife, that he might have children; and no one prays for what he despairs of obtaining — as he had so despaired that he would not believe the promise even from an angel. The words must therefore be understood of the people; and since their salvation and the putting away of their sins was to be through Christ, a son is announced to Zacharias because that son was ordained to be Christ's forerunner.

Gill places the crowd in the court of the Israelites and infers from its size that this may well have been a sabbath, since on an ordinary day only the priests and Levites of the course, the stationary men and some of the more devout would have been there. He identifies the messenger as Gabriel, the same who had appeared to Daniel about the evening oblation nearly five hundred years before.

Clarke draws the correspondence tighter: the incense was itself an emblem of the prayers of God's people, so that while the priest performs the rite the people are employed in the thing signified — happy the people who attend to the spirit as well as the letter of every divine institution. He finds every circumstance significant: that an angel should appear at all, when neither prophecy nor angelic ministry had been vouchsafed for some four hundred years; that he was sent to a priest, whose office pointed out the Son of God until he came; that it happened at Jerusalem rather than the hill country, so that there should be witnesses; and that it fell at the solemn hour of public prayer. Wesley says the practice was the constant one of the pious Jews, and the foundation of that elegant figure by which prayer is so often compared to incense.

Robertson finds the whole posture in one periphrastic imperfect, the crowd at prayer outside while the clouds of incense rose within; on the appearance he notes that the verb is the very form Paul uses of the resurrection appearances, and refuses the softening options — we must choose, with Plummer, between admitting an objective appearance and calling the whole a myth. Ellicott explains why the position of the altar mattered, standing immediately before the veil dividing the outer sanctuary from the Holy of Holies, of shittim wood overlaid with gold, both symbols of incorruption, so closely connected with the inner chamber that the writer to the Hebrews seems to reckon it as belonging there. He reaches Augustine's conclusion from the other end of the temple, since the prayers of the crowd no less than the priest's turned toward the manifestation of the kingdom, and in it stood the aged Simeon and Anna the prophetess and many others who waited for redemption in Jerusalem.

12.pericope_label: Fear not, Zacharias, for thy prayer is heard

schools.summary: Gill accounts for the terror by rarity, since such appearances were not now so common as formerly, and even when they were more usual they generally had this effect on the minds of good men. Calvin turns the fear into a doctrine and then withdraws its sting: God does not appear to his servants in order to terrify them, yet it is advantageous and even necessary that they be struck with awe, so that amid their agitation they learn to give God the glory due to his name. His presence humbles the pride of the flesh, which is so insolent that men never submit until overcome by force; whence it is only when they have withdrawn from his presence that they indulge in self-flattery. But the glory of God is not so appalling to the saints as to swallow them up, only to cast them down from a foolish confidence, and as soon as he has abased the pride of the flesh in those who believe he stretches out his hand to raise them up. They are greatly mistaken, Calvin adds, who hide themselves from the face of God in order to enjoy peace. On the prayer he agrees it is hardly probable that Zacharias then prayed for a child he had despaired of, and settles for the reading that a prayer long poured out was at length heard; and on the name he holds it was given to heighten the authority of the office, commending not the grace bestowed on the man privately but the grace his mission would bring to all.

Clarke supplies a reason nearer the bone for the fear, that Zacharias dreaded a messenger come to denounce the judgments of God against a faithless and disobedient people who had too long and too well merited them. On the prayer he will have both: the words refer to the prayers Zacharias had offered for a son and to those for the deliverance of Israel, and they are all heard — from which he draws the comfort that fervent prayers not immediately answered are not lost but registered in heaven. Wesley finds a mercy in the ordinary invisibility of such servants, since a man accustomed to converse with God was here thrown into consternation, nature not being able to sustain the sight.

Ellicott says that in all the long years of his ministration Zacharias had seen no such manifestation, and guesses at the form from the analogy of other angelic appearances — a young man clothed in white linen, a kind of transfigured Levite. On the prayer he takes the opposite line to Clarke, that the hope of a son had died out long before and the prayer implied is that the Kingdom of God might come, so that praying for this the man receives more than he asks. Robertson thinks it probably was the prayer for a son, in spite of Elisabeth's great age, though he allows the Messianic redemption as possible.

14.pericope_label: He shall be great in the sight of the Lord

schools.summary: Gill answers that the greatness was not of birth and blood or of worldly riches, but of gifts and grace, of work and office and usefulness. Calvin will not let the promised joy shrink to a nursery: the angel describes a gladness greater than the birth of a child could give, and one not confined within private walls but shared by strangers, a son born not to Zacharias only but as Teacher and Prophet of the whole people. He turns sharply on those who have made the verse a warrant for keeping the Baptist's birthday with processions and dancing and licence, since the angel restricts his commendation to the joy godly men would take in the man's instruction. On the abstinence he says the words are meant less to extol eminent virtues than to proclaim a glorious office, and that the fasting was no singular virtue but a visible token by which the world might acknowledge a lifelong Nazarite — from which he refuses the obvious application, that the worship of God consists in abstaining from wine, as apish copyists pick some part of the fathers' actions for imitation.

Clarke traces the word for strong drink to the Hebrew verb meaning to inebriate, quotes Jerome that any inebriating liquor is called sicera whether made of corn, apples, honey or dates, and derives our own cyder from it; he also reports a reading followed by one manuscript, two versions and four of the primitive fathers which puts the filling with the Spirit in the womb rather than from it, and asks whether it did not take place at the salutation of the Virgin. Wesley makes the two halves one thing: exemplary in self-denial, and so much the more filled with the Holy Ghost.

Barnes takes trouble to disarm a false inference about the drink. The wine commonly drunk in Judea was a light wine, often no stronger than cider, and the common drink of every class, forbidden to the Nazarite alone; and the second term cannot mean strong drink in our sense, since distilled spirits were not then known, the art having been discovered by an Arabian chemist centuries later — and distilled liquors are not used by Arabians at all, who banished them as if sensible of their pernicious influence, while Europe and America are where the poison has ruined millions. Ellicott sets the vow in its line of descent, a Nazarite for life and the representative of the separated form of a consecrated life, what Samson had been and probably Samuel, and reads the abstinence as making room for something: the absence of the lower stimulation implied a capacity for the higher enthusiasm which is the gift of God. Robertson puts that contrast in a phrase, the Holy Spirit set over against the physical excitement of strong drink.

16.pericope_label: Many of the children of Israel shall he turn, in the spirit and power of Elias

schools.summary: Gill holds the prediction verified precisely because the word is many and not all, since great multitudes flocked to John while some slighted his preaching. Calvin reads a darker fact out of the same word: those in whom conversion could take place must have been apostates, so the verse shows how dissolute the Church then was, and if the ancient Church could be so far gone it is a frivolous pretext by which the Papists defend their own superstitions when they say the Church cannot err. He then faces the difficulty that the promise seems to give a man more than a man can do, since conversion is a greater work than the creation of men, and answers that when the Lord bestows such praise on the outward doctrine he does not separate it from the secret influence of his Spirit; ministers are nothing more than the hand of God. He adds a proof from the record itself: it plainly does not lie in the minister's power to bring men back, since John did not indiscriminately bring all back, as he unquestionably would have done had everything yielded to his wish. On the Elijah clause Calvin warns against indulging a dream like that of Pythagoras, as though the prophet's soul had passed into John's body, when what is meant is that the same Spirit exerted a like power in the Baptist.

Wesley takes the practical encouragement, that none need be ashamed of preaching like John the Baptist. Clarke traces the resemblance to Elijah in the austere manner of life and the zeal that reproved even princes, and reads the turning of hearts as a figure in which the patriarchs, alienated from their children by unbelief, are brought to look on them again with delight — though some, he reports, take the fathers for the Jews and the children for the Gentiles.

Ellicott hears where the sentence comes from: the opening words of the message of the New Covenant spring out of the closing words of the last of the prophets, and point to that revival of the Elijah ministry which the next verse announces outright. Barnes glosses the turning as repentance, and says the connection leads us to suppose the pronoun in the next verse refers to the Lord their God — from which it follows that the Messiah was the Lord God of Israel. Robertson agrees it must be the Lord their God, since the Messiah has not yet been mentioned, and notes that John himself will deny being Elijah in person while Jesus will call him Elijah in spirit; on the turning of hearts he prefers a plainer sense, that paternal love had died out and its revival in the home is among the first results of conversion.

18.pericope_label: Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man

schools.summary: Chrysostom states the two grounds of the doubt as the man himself would have felt them: his own age and his wife's barrenness, an unseasonable time of life and an ill-suited nature, the planter infirm and the soil barren. He reports at once that some think the objection unpardonable in a priest, since when God declares anything it becomes us to receive it in faith, and disputes of this kind are the mark of a rebellious spirit.

Gill sharpens the ingratitude — that after such an appearance, in such a place, and with these things given as the return of his own prayer, he still wanted a sign, as the Jews were generally desirous of doing. Calvin raises the harder question, which is not why Zacharias doubted but why he alone was punished for it: Abraham brought forward his old age in the same way and is applauded for it, Gideon was not blamed for asking a sign twice, and Mary's own objection follows a few verses later and is passed over as if it contained nothing wrong. If the words alone are weighed, Calvin concedes, either all were equally to blame or Zacharias did nothing wrong; his answer is that words and actions must be judged from the state of the heart, and the Lord beheld in Zacharias something worse than his words will bear — the same discrimination by which God distinguishes Sarah's laugh from Abraham's. What the something worse was he then names: stopping at the ordinary course of nature, Zacharias ascribed less than he ought to the power of God. Yet Calvin will not make the failure total, since there is a general faith which embraces eternal salvation and beside it many special promises with a special faith answering to each, so that the branches of faith may be agitated by tempests without its giving way at the root.

Wesley draws the comparison the chapter itself invites, that Zacharias disbelieved the fact while Mary had no doubt of the thing and inquired only about the manner. Clarke leaves the sternest verdict: no natural impediment has any power once God has declared his purpose, and it is impious, when we are convinced that a word is his, to demand a pledge for its fulfilment.

Robertson glosses the question as according to what and puts it plainly: it was too good to be true, so the man who had prayed for the blessing turned sceptical when it came, like the disciples in the house of Mary who would not believe Peter stood at the door. Barnes allows the thing was improbable and evidence natural to desire, but holds that the testimony of an angel in such a place should have been proof enough, and that men are simply slow to believe heavenly messengers.

19.pericope_label: I am Gabriel; and, behold, thou shalt be dumb

schools.summary: Gill reports the Jewish account that the names of angels came up out of Babylon by means of the Israelites, and that it was there Daniel became acquainted with both Gabriel and Michael; he judges that since Syriac was generally understood among the Jews at the time, the angel probably used it. He turns the negative of the next verse into a general rule: there is no reason to stagger at any promise of God, since the promises are made by one who cannot lie, every promise is in Christ yea and amen, and never yet did one of them fail. Calvin turns the rebuke outward — what had been questioned was not the messenger's veracity but the veracity of God who sent him, so that the author of the promise was treated with indignity in the person of his ambassador; and the name is given for our sakes rather than the angel's, to instruct us that we must not ascribe to angels anything of their own. On the punishment he thinks it peculiarly fitted to the fault, since a man who had interrupted the promise with murmurs ought to have heard it in silence: faith has its silence, to lend an ear to the Word of God, and afterwards its turn to speak and answer Amen. Yet he finds the sentence mitigated in two ways, by its limited term and by the promise not being withdrawn.

Clarke finds the name itself suited to the occasion, being compounded of the words for might and for God, and so pointing to the all-prevailing power by which the strong God could accomplish every purpose. On the silence he observes that this was not the ordinary dumbness proceeding from some weakness in the organs of speech, since there was no such weakness here; silence was imposed, and he should not be able to break it until the power that silenced him gave leave — let those who are intemperate with their tongues behold both the severity and the mercy of the Lord in nine months' silence for one intemperate speech. Wesley hears a deliberate gradation in the self-description, enhancing the guilt step by step: I am Gabriel, a holy angel; yea, one of the highest order; not only so, but now peculiarly sent from God; and that with a message to you in particular.

Ellicott notes how late angelic names are, none appearing in the Old Testament until after the Babylonian exile and then Gabriel, Michael and Raphael together; since Gabriel had appeared in the prophecies which more than any others were the germ of the Messianic expectations, there was a fitness in his being sent now. He catches the irony of the sign exactly: the demand had implied a want of faith, and so the sign took the form of a penalty. Barnes renders the name man of God, recalls that this was the angel deputed to tell Daniel his prayers were heard, and calls the dumbness both a sign that the angel had come from God and a judgment for not crediting it — there being no sin, he says, more aggravated in the sight of God than unbelief. Robertson says the whole self-description is a rebuke to the doubt.

outliers.note: reads the punishment as fitted to the fault, since faith has its own silence for hearing the Word before it has its turn to answer Amen

the insult offered in the person of the messenger
a sign that is also a penalty

21.pericope_label: The people waited for Zacharias, and marvelled that he tarried

schools.summary: Gill offers three guesses at the excess of time: a longer conversation than Luke reports, or amazement at the sight that kept him musing, or time given to mental prayer and confession and thanksgiving. Calvin's interest is that the delay made the people witnesses. Zacharias had tarried beyond the usual time, which of itself suggests something uncommon; when he came out he made known by looks and gestures that he had been struck dumb, and there is reason to think there were traces of alarm in his countenance as well. From these obvious symptoms they concluded that God had appeared to him, and Calvin thinks the inference sound: it was no common accident but rather an astonishing work of God that a man should become suddenly dumb without disease and emerge, after a more than ordinary delay, in a state of amazement. He grants that there were few or no visions in that age, but the people remembered that in the time of their fathers such things had been frequent.

Clarke fills in what the half hour held — a profound silence, the people standing without engaged in mental prayer — and observes that Zacharias had spent not only the time the incense required but whatever the discourse with the angel took up besides; he also explains why the crowd had seen nothing, the sanctuary being divided from the court by a great veil, so that they understood only from the man's own signs. Wesley says what the crowd was waiting for, to be dismissed with the blessing.

Barnes reports that a priest was not accustomed to remain in the temple more than about half an hour, so that when this one stayed longer the people grew apprehensive for his safety; he glosses the noun as sight or appearance, commonly applied to spirits or beings from another world. Robertson cites the Talmud to the same effect about the brief time in the sanctuary, notes that the verb for waiting is an old word denoting mental direction whether of hope or fear, and finds the decisive evidence in what was missing — they knew clearly because he could not pronounce the benediction. Ellicott points out that the word for what they perceived is chosen as distinguished from a dream, to imply that what had been witnessed was seen with the waking sense, and that the look of awe, the strange gestures and the unwonted silence together showed the man had come under the influence of some supernatural power.

outliers.note: treats the delay itself as providential, since it turned an unseen event inside the sanctuary into something the whole waiting congregation could infer from visible symptoms

themes: how long a priest was expected to stay within
the crowd as witnesses of the vision
a vision distinguished from a dream

23.pericope_label: He departed to his own house, and Elisabeth conceived and hid herself

schools.summary: Chrysostom hears only the reversal: the unfruitful rock has produced the green blade, and her joy is twofold, the mark of barrenness taken away and an illustrious offspring given — for in other births there is the coming together of parents, while this birth was the effect of heavenly grace.

Gill notes that three months was the term the Jewish doctors laid down for determining whether a woman was with child, as in cases of divorce or death, and that Elisabeth knew the story already, her husband having informed her by writing. Calvin uses the going home to explain the staying away: so long as the priests were attending in their courses they did not enter their own houses, galleries having been built round the temple walls where they had chambers, and they were discharged not only from their wives but from wine and strong drink. On that second half he turns the whole argument against the law of celibacy, since those who plead this precedent for perpetual continence should say why they do not also abstain from wine, we not being at liberty to separate commandments God has joined. The real solution lies in the distinction between law and gospel: a priest then stood before God to expiate the people's sins, a figure of the true Mediator, and needed something peculiar to mark him off — the design of the holy garments and the anointing — whereas the pastors Christ appointed have nothing of the kind, and may rest in the decision of the Spirit that marriage is honourable in all. On the concealment he rejects the suggestion that Elisabeth doubted and feared ridicule, and offers two other reasons: that until the work was manifest she might hesitate to expose it to the diversified opinions of men, and that when she was discovered all at once to be with child men would be the more moved to praise God.

Clarke observes that had Zacharias not loved the service, the loss of his speech would have made an excellent pretext for leaving at once, and turns on his own profession: preachers who abandon the vineyard for some trifling bodily disorder show either that they never had a proper concern for their Master's honour or that they have lost his spirit. Wesley thinks Elisabeth retired for leisure to bless God.

Barnes says the occurrence and his own calamity might well have sent Zacharias home, but his duty was in the temple, and ministers are to remain at their work until genuinely unfitted for it. Ellicott notes that the word for the ministration carries the idea of liturgical service, the days running from sabbath to sabbath, and on the reproach says the words express the Jewish feeling about maternity in almost its strongest form, childlessness being more than a misfortune and seeming to imply some secret sin God was punishing. Robertson traces the word for ministration to our liturgy, and cites Hobart's remark that Luke has almost as many words for pregnancy and barrenness as Hippocrates.

26.pericope_label: The angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin espoused to Joseph

schools.summary: Chrysostom explains the timing: the angel comes before the conception rather than after, lest she be too much troubled, and stands by her in visible shape rather than in a dream, since tidings so great needed an extraordinary manifestation before the event.

Cyril uses the betrothal against two errors at once, refusing both those who teach that Christ's coming was a phantom and those who say his birth was of husband and wife: Mary is called Joseph's wife because betrothed to him, as Rachel was called Jacob's wife before the wedded state, merely because there was a promise.

Gill reads the interval as a measure of rank, six months separating the two conceptions and the two births, with John going before Christ as man while Christ was preferred before him as mediator. Calvin finds in the arrangement something far removed from the ordinary judgment of men — that God should make the beginning of the herald's generation more illustrious than that of his own Son, the prophecy about John being published in the temple and universally known while Christ is promised to a virgin in an obscure town and the promise stays buried in the breast of a young woman. It was proper that from his birth the saying should hold, that it pleased God by foolishness to save them that believe. On the betrothal he reads the marriage as a veil held before the eyes of the world, though he rejects Origen's notion that the purpose was to hide the coming salvation from Satan.

Henry finds providence in the obscurity of the town: a remote corner, in no reputation for religion or learning, bordering on the heathen and so called Galilee of the Gentiles, so that Christ's having his relations there intimates favour in reserve for the Gentile world — no disadvantage of place shall prejudice those for whom God has favours in store. He takes the name as Miriam's, signifying exalted, and the lineage as royal though poor.

Clarke raises the question the address invites — since Joseph and Mary were both of David's family, whose estate lay in Bethlehem, why was the household not there? — and answers that they probably withdrew to Galilee for fear of Herod's jealousy, who had usurped a throne to which they had an indisputable right. Wesley notes that the reckoning dates from Elisabeth's conceiving.

Ellicott notes that the reckoning runs from the period named two verses earlier, and describes the town at length: a valley among hills that rise some five hundred feet on the north of the Plain of Esdraelon, richly cultivated, the slopes clothed in spring with flowers, one side broken by a steep ridge that forms something like a precipice, with one of the finest views in Palestine from the hill behind it; the name he derives from the Hebrew word for a branch. Barnes marks the month and the town without comment; Robertson, that Gabriel is God's messenger to Mary as to Zacharias.

outliers.note: notes the inversion by which the forerunner's birth is announced in the temple before the nation while the Messiah's is entrusted to a single young woman in an obscure town, and reads it as God saving by what the world counts foolishness

themes: the herald announced more publicly than the Son
Nazareth and why the family was there
virgin and espoused at once

27.pericope_label: Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee

schools.summary: Gill puts the scene plainly, that the angel came into her house and into the room where she was. Calvin explains why grace should head the message at all: our capacities admit too slender a portion of knowledge to comprehend the greatness of God's works, so the angel first prepares the heart by meditation on undeserved favour and then enlarges it to receive an incomprehensible mystery, a conviction of the Divine goodness being the entrance of faith. From which he draws his conclusion: if Mary's happiness and righteousness flow from the undeserved love of God, and her excellence is nothing more than the Divine kindness, it is the height of absurdity to seek from her what she derives from the same quarter as ourselves — the words being a simple congratulation, which those who have turned them into a prayer both misuse and address to a person who is absent.

Clarke refuses to dissolve the visit into a dream, since divine visions are announced as such in the sacred writings, and states the limit as sharply as Calvin — highly favoured as chosen before all women to be the mother of the Messiah, not the mother of God, which he calls blasphemy. Wesley works through the parallels, that what is said here of favour was said of Noah and Moses and David, that the Lord is with thee was said to Gideon, and that Jael was called blessed above women.

Ellicott is careful to say how little is known of Mary: the canonical Gospels tell us nothing of her parentage, and the apocryphal legends have left their impress on Christian art without any claim to the character even of tradition; the scanty notices are that she was a kinswoman of Elisabeth, and so possibly of the daughters of Aaron, and that she had a sister, while the silence about her parents suggests an orphan and the narrative presupposes poverty. On the disputed participle he says the verb is the same elsewhere translated hath made us accepted, and that the rendering full of grace has no warrant in the meaning of the word; he notes too that the closing clause is omitted in many of the best manuscripts. Robertson adds the legal weight of the betrothal, which usually lasted a year and under which unfaithfulness in the bride was punished with death, glosses the perfect passive as endowed with grace, and reports that the oldest manuscripts carry the blessing not here but later in the chapter. Barnes takes the greeting as equivalent to peace be with thee and observes that the verb is absent from the next clause in the Greek, so that it may as well be read as the angel's prayer.

29.pericope_label: Thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and shalt call his name JESUS

schools.summary: Chrysostom answers those who find it unworthy that God should inhabit a body by pointing at the sun, whose heat is felt by every body that receives its rays without its own purity being sullied — much more does the Sun of Righteousness, taking a pure body from the Virgin's womb, escape defilement and show forth his mother in greater holiness.

Gill marks the interjection that opens the promise, a conception in a pure virgin being matter for a behold, and notes that the Persic and the Vulgate differ over whether she saw the angel or heard him. Calvin observes that Luke ascribes the trouble to the words rather than the presence, and asks why the presence should be mentioned at all, answering that she was seized with dread arising out of reverence for God — though Luke does not say she lost her recollection, but on the contrary records a mark of an attentive and composed mind. He makes the fear general before removing it: whenever the feeblest ray of the Divine glory bursts upon us we cannot avoid alarm, since we cannot apprehend the presence of God apart from its effects, and the virgin saw in her own nation such a mass of crimes that she had reason to dread heavier punishments. On the name he thinks the angel deliberately adapted his words to Isaiah and other passages esteemed among the godly, and finds the one word conceive enough to set aside the dream of Marcion and Manichaeus, since Mary brought forth no ethereal body or phantom but the fruit she had carried.
Clarke says the glorious appearance left her puzzled to find the purport of the speech.

Ellicott notes that the word for her trouble is the one used of Zacharias, so that with her as with him the first feeling was natural terror, and prefers to keep the rendering favour rather than grace, the latter word being fit enough but now bound up with the technicalities of theology. He observes that Luke makes no reference to Isaiah's prophecy, though Mary's answer shows she understood the angel in the sense Matthew gives the prophet's words, and that what perplexed her was that conception and birth should be spoken of in a prediction which said nothing of her approaching marriage. Barnes accounts for the trouble by accumulation — so unexpected, so sudden, so extraordinary, and so high an honour that she was filled with anxious thoughts — and hears in the opening words the reassurance that the messenger brings good tidings. Robertson finds both states in the tenses, that she was upset and then reckoned up the reasons, and traces the noun for favour to the root of the verb to rejoice, its senses beginning in sweetness and delight and carrying the notion of kindness, especially of God toward men.

outliers.note: finds in the single word conceive a sufficient answer to Marcion and Manichaeus, since it makes the child the fruit already carried rather than an ethereal body or phantom

themes: trouble at the words rather than the presence
favour rather than grace
the conception no phantom

32.pericope_label: He shall be called the Son of the Highest, and the Lord shall give him the throne of David

schools.summary: Cyril meets the objection directly: if any denies the promise because Christ never sat on David's wooden throne, let him remember that the scribes sit in Moses' seat, which signifies not a wooden seat but the authority of his teaching — so seek for David's throne not the timber but the kingdom itself. The discourse is plainly of Christ and not of Solomon, whose throne did not endure as the sun.

Gill divides the greatness by office: great in his person as God-man; great in the prophetic office, as that prophet Moses spoke of; great as high priest, both in the oblation of himself and in his prevailing intercession; great as king; and great in his works. Calvin presses against those who would soften the title. The angel had said something similar of John without making him equal to Christ, since the Baptist is great in his own class while the greatness of Christ raises him above all creatures; angels and kings are so dignified in Scripture, but in common and on account of their rank, whereas God distinguishes his own Son by addressing him particularly, and we are sons by adoption obtained through faith, he the only-begotten. Calvin uses this against Servetus, who argued from the future tense that Christ began to be the Son of God only when he took our flesh: the words mean that he who had been the Son from eternity would be manifested as such in the flesh, there being a wide difference between beginning to be what one was not and being made known as what one already was. He observes too that the prophets always direct the hope of believers to the kingdom of David, so that it became a Jewish maxim that the safety of the church hung on that kingdom's prosperity.

Clarke reaches four heads of his own: that the human nature born of the virgin was to be united with the divine; that it should be called in a peculiar sense the Son of the most high God, since God would produce it in her womb without the intervention of man; that he should be everlasting Head of his Church; and that his kingdom should be eternal, his being the only dominion that shall never have an end. Wesley says only that the title belongs to him in a more eminent sense than any man or angel can claim.

Robertson notes there is no article in the Greek, and since sons of the Most High is used elsewhere of men we cannot insist on deity here, though it remains possible. Ellicott adds that the same title is afterwards heard on the lips of the demoniacs, and says the words about the throne at first suggest that the Virgin was herself of the house of David and the title came through her; on the other hand both genealogies appear to give the lineage of Joseph only. He adds that the promise, which might well have raised the expectation of a revived kingdom of Israel, is among the most memorable instances of a prophecy fulfilled in quite another fashion than its first hearers could have imagined. Barnes keeps to the plain sense: great in power, in wisdom, in dominion on earth and in heaven.

33.pericope_label: How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?

schools.summary: Cyril lets the wonder stand where it fell: she who bore him wondered at it herself, and the generation was immaculate and undefiled, for where the Holy Spirit breathes all pollution is taken away.

Gill insists she did not doubt: she required no sign as Zacharias did, is nowhere charged with unbelief, and is expressly said to have believed — her words express amazement and a wish to know the manner. On the kingdom he refuses a literal reading of the house named, taking it not of the natural posterity of Jacob but of the whole Israel of God consisting of Jews and Gentiles. Calvin alone will not let Mary off. She appears to confine the power of God within as narrow limits as Zacharias did, concluding what lies beyond the common order of nature to be impossible, when she ought to have risen at once by faith to a power not fettered by natural means; we need not, he says, take much trouble to acquit her. Yet he grants she does not lower God's power to the level of her senses, but is carried away by a sudden impulse of astonishment, and that her embracing the promise appears from her hesitating on one point only. He also rejects as unfounded and altogether absurd the inference that she had vowed perpetual virginity, since she would then have dealt treacherously in allowing herself to be given to a husband — and it is idle to suppose a monastic life existed among the Jews. On the throne he explains that it was erected among Israel that Christ might thence subdue the whole world, and that by a new adoption God has admitted the Gentiles who were formerly strangers.
Clarke takes the house of Jacob of all who belong to the twelve tribes; Wesley says in which all true believers are included.

Ellicott sets the questions side by side: Zacharias asked by what sign he should know the words were true, whereas Mary, told of a far greater marvel and understanding the birth to be antecedent to her marriage, accepts the words in faith and seeks only to know how they will be accomplished. On the perpetuity of the kingdom he states both halves of the difficulty — that the apparent promise is of a kingdom restored to Israel, such as the disciples still expected after the Resurrection, and that Paul's language elsewhere seems at first to fix a term to the kingdom of the Christ, though closer study shows he speaks of it as a contest with the hostile forces of evil, so that the sovereignty ceases by being perfected and not by passing away. Barnes reads the phrase as equivalent to saying he would reign over his own church for ever, and presses the last clause: his is the only kingdom that shall never have an end. Robertson observes that Luke reports the perpetuity without any Pauline interpretation of a spiritual Israel, though that was the true meaning and Luke knew it.

35.pericope_label: The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee; that holy thing shall be called the Son of God

schools.summary: Gill notes that the angel now gives an account of the manner, with things to strengthen her faith. Calvin warns it is not designed to satisfy curiosity: it leads the virgin to contemplate the power of the Spirit and surrender herself silently to his guidance. The first verb denotes an extraordinary work in which natural means have no place; the second carries an elegant metaphor, for though God's protection is often likened to a shadow, the sense here seems peculiar — the Spirit's operation would be secret, as if an intervening cloud forbade it to be seen by men. Calvin then answers the argument drawn from the word therefore. Those who imagine Christ became the Son of God after his human generation seize on this very particle; but the conclusion is false, for though he was manifested to be the Son of God in the flesh it does not follow that he was not the Word begotten of the Father before the ages, and the name, which belonged to the divine essence from the beginning, is now applied unitedly to both natures. He explains the word holy in a practical way: as Christ had to be a real man, to expiate our sins in our flesh, so he had to be free from every spot if he was to cleanse others.

Clarke presses the opposite case as far as it will go. The angel does not give the appellation to the divine nature at all, but to that holy thing which was to be born of the virgin, since the divine nature could not be born and had no beginning; and he says outright that the doctrine of the eternal Sonship seems to him anti-scriptural and highly dangerous, since son implies a father and so precedency in time — the phrase eternal Son being, in his judgement, a positive self-contradiction. He also agrees that the allusion is to the Spirit brooding on the waters, confirming his view that Christ's human nature was a real creation in the womb. Wesley holds both halves together: the power of the Highest was exerted by the Spirit as his own, and the title belongs to Christ not only as he is God from eternity but on this account likewise.

Barnes takes the passage to prove beyond controversy that one reason Jesus was called the Son of God is that he was begotten in a supernatural manner; the body was created by the direct power of God because a Messiah atoning for others and not himself needed a human nature free from the corruption of the fall. Ellicott holds a middle position: the words do appear to rest the title on the supernatural birth rather than the eternal pre-existence, and we may accept that the angel's message was a partial and not a complete revelation, giving a sufficient reason for the name and no more than was then required. Robertson takes the figure of overshadowing the other way, the verb being used of the bright cloud at the Transfiguration, and hears in it the Shekinah glory, where the cloud represents the presence and power of God; he adds that the phrase was in any case a recognised designation of the Messiah.

36.pericope_label: With God nothing shall be impossible: behold the handmaid of the Lord

schools.summary: Chrysostom admires the tact of the sign: the previous words had overcome the mind of the virgin, so the angel drops to a humbler subject and persuades her by sensible things; he did not remind her of Sarah or Rebecca or Rachel, examples of ancient times, but brought forward a recent event, to strike her mind the more forcibly. For the same reason he named the age and the natural infirmity, and spoke not at the beginning of Elisabeth's conception but after six months, when the swelling of the womb could confirm it.

Gill explains that Elisabeth might be of Levi by her father and of Judah by her mother, intermarriage between the tribes being frequent and no offence against the intention of the law, which forbade it in order to preserve each tribe's inheritance — a danger that did not arise where Levi had no inheritance at all. Calvin reasons from the same instance: if neither barrenness nor old age could prevent God from making Elisabeth a mother, Mary had no reason to confine her view within the ordinary limits of nature; and the month is named because a woman usually feels the child quicken in the fifth, so the sixth removes all doubt. He uses the closing maxim to correct a habit of mind. Taken strictly it means that God will do what he has promised, since no hindrance can resist his power; and they wander widely from the truth who imagine the power of God to be something lying beyond his word, for it is idle and even dangerous to argue what God can do without taking into account what he resolves to do. What the angel does here God frequently does in Scripture — employ a general doctrine to confirm one particular promise, since promises in their general form make little impression on us. On the answer that follows Calvin notes that the virgin stops the entrance of opposing arguments and compels herself to obey, which is the real proof of faith, boldness in disputing being the mother of unbelief.

Clarke hears in the angel's closing maxim the words spoken to Sarah when the birth of Isaac was foretold, and thinks Mary could not have missed the allusion. Wesley states the legal point more narrowly: the law forbade only heiresses to marry outside their tribe, so that others intermarried continually, particularly the families of David and Levi.

Ellicott infers from the word for kinswoman that either a parent of Mary was of the house of Aaron or the mother of Elisabeth of the house of David; on Mary's answer he hears more than submission — a half-consciousness that the lot she accepts may bring unknown sufferings as well as untold blessedness, so that she shrinks from the awfulness of the position and yet can say what her Son would say in his own hour, not my will but thine be done. Robertson cuts the knot on the kinship: the word need not mean cousin, but simply relative. Barnes says the case of Elisabeth was mentioned to inspire confidence, being almost as improbable as Mary's own, and reads the final words as resignation and faith at once.

outliers.note: warns against separating the power of God from his word, holding it idle and even dangerous to argue what God can do without also asking what he has resolved to do

39.pericope_label: Mary arose and went into the hill country with haste

schools.summary: Gill has her setting out as soon as the angel was gone, partly to use the sign she had been given, and partly to talk with Elisabeth of what God had done for each of them. Calvin takes the journey as evidence about the faith that preceded it: the promise did not fade away with the presence of the angel but was impressed on her mind, and the haste indicates a sincere and strong affection. He asks what her object was and rejects two answers — it was not mere inquiry, since she already cherished by faith the Son of God conceived in her womb, nor was it, as some think, to congratulate her kinswoman; more probably it was partly to strengthen her own faith and partly to celebrate the grace of God which both of them had received, for though believers are satisfied with the bare word of God they do not disregard any of his works that help to confirm it. On the city he will say only what Luke says, that it belonged to the tribe of Judah and stood in a hilly district, from which he infers that it lay farther from Nazareth than Jerusalem did.

Henry notices the courtesy of the arrangement: Mary was the younger and the younger with child, so if they were to meet it was fittest she should travel, not insisting on the preference her conception gave her; and she went with care and expedition, not as young people commonly go abroad to visit friends, to divert herself, but to inform herself. He reports at length a conjecture of Lightfoot's which he plainly finds attractive — that Mary was to conceive our Saviour at Hebron itself, that she may have been given some intimation of it, and that this is why she made such haste. It suits the harmony God uses in his works, on that view, that Shiloh of the tribe of Judah should be conceived in a city of Judah and of David, as he was to be born in Bethlehem; and Hebron was where the promise was given to Isaac and circumcision instituted, where Abraham had his first land and David his first crown, and where the three patriarchal couples lay interred. Henry sees no improbability in it and adds a support of his own, that Elisabeth says there shall be a performance, as though it were not performed yet but was to be performed there. From the visit he draws the general rule that those who have a good work of grace begun in them do well to consult others in the same case and compare experiences, since as in water face answers to face, so does the heart of man to man.

Clarke names Hebron, the city of the priests in the tribe of Judah, some forty miles south of Jerusalem and upwards of seventy from Nazareth; Wesley agrees, adding that it belonged to the house of Aaron.

Barnes declines to guess — some have supposed Jerusalem and others Hebron, but all is conjecture, and the most that can be said is that it was probably a Levitical city where Zacharias lived when off duty. Ellicott finds the description too vague to identify, notes that no city of the name is known, and offers Juttah, near Maon and the Judaean Carmel and so in the hill country; he adds the reflection that the journey brought the Virgin not far from the place where she was to give birth. Robertson observes that the word Luke uses for the hill country is an old one found in the Septuagint but nowhere else in the New Testament, and allows the same guess, that Judah here may stand for Juttah.

40.pericope_label: The babe leaped in her womb, and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost

schools.summary: Cyril takes the scene as the Spirit's own work, remarking that he recognises not virgins only but matrons also.

Gill notices whom Mary did not greet — Zacharias, either because he was not at home, or because being deaf and dumb he could neither hear nor return it, or because it was not usual for women to salute men. Calvin will not go as far as Clarke on the leaping. He grants that sudden joy in a pregnant woman naturally moves the child, and holds that Luke means something extraordinary here; but he refuses the intricate questions, whether the infant was aware of Christ's presence or felt an emotion of piety, since Luke does not say the feeling belonged to the child, and rather intimates that this part of the divine operation took place in the mother. The filling he understands as a sudden endowment with prophecy to an unusual degree. On the blessing he raises an objection to the sentence: Elisabeth seems to put Mary and Christ on an equal footing, which would be highly improper — his answer being that the second clause assigns the reason for the first, with the qualification that to carry Christ in her womb was not Mary's first blessedness, being far inferior to being born again by the Spirit. He praises the happy medium Elisabeth keeps, since the world's native depravity is such that few escape one of two faults: some, delighted with themselves, enviously despise the gifts of God in their brethren, while others praise those gifts so superstitiously as to turn them into idols — with the result that the first rank is assigned to Mary and Christ lowered as it were to the footstool.

Clarke takes the leaping as the accomplishment of the earlier promise that the child should be filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother's womb: the mother is filled, and the child within her becomes sensible of the divine influence. Wesley says the joy of her soul so affected her body that the child was moved as if it leaped for joy.

Ellicott supposes the words of the greeting were the ordinary formula, peace be with thee, perhaps joined to some congratulation on what she had heard from the angel, and adds that, so far as human sources go, the account of a scene between two women alone must have reached Luke from the Virgin herself. On the blessing he hears the poetry of the older Scriptures and notes the contrast between the same phrase applied there to the murderess Jael and here to the mother of the Lord; and he thinks the contrast leaves no doubt that Elisabeth used the word Lord in its highest sense. Robertson finds more in the greeting: her first glance at Elisabeth showed the truth of the angel's message, and the two mothers had a bond of sympathy; he keeps the middle ground on the leaping, which is common enough, holding that it was the Spirit's filling that let Elisabeth understand what had happened. Barnes lists what the filling produced — joy, a disposition to praise God, and prophetic knowledge of the child — and is more cautious about the word Lord, which may denote divinity or merely a superior.

45.pericope_label: Blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance

schools.summary: Gill sets the two believers of the chapter against each other and makes the comparison exact: Mary was a very young woman, told things incredible to nature and reason, and she believed without objecting or asking a sign; Zacharias was a man in years, a priest by office, and he was incredulous about something far more possible, since there had been instances before in Sarah, in Hannah and in the wife of Manoah, whereas of a virgin's conceiving there had been none. Calvin takes the sense that faith gives way to the divine promises so that they may obtain their accomplishment in us, and is careful to say what that does not mean: the truth of God does not depend on the will of men, and he remains true though the whole world should try to ruin his veracity; but since unbelievers are unworthy to obtain the fruit of the promises, Scripture teaches that by faith alone they are made powerful for our salvation. God offers his benefits indiscriminately to all, and faith holds out its lap to receive them, while unbelief lets them pass by without reaching us. On the last words he notes that the promise had been brought by an angel and yet proceeded from God alone, whence God wishes his Word to be paid equal honour whether he employs the ministrations of angels or of men.

Clarke prefers the reading that makes the clause the content of her faith rather than its ground: faith is here the foundation of true happiness because it receives the fulfilment of God's promises, and since whatever God has promised he intends to perform, his own authority is reason enough to believe. Wesley thinks it probable that Elisabeth had her husband's unbelief in mind as she spoke.

Ellicott says the two renderings, for there shall be and that there shall be, are equally tenable on grammatical grounds, but that internal considerations favour the second, since the first appears to make the fulfilment of the promise depend on the Virgin's faith. Robertson leaves it open, since it makes good sense either way, and notes that this is the first beatitude in the New Testament, answering to the last one in the Gospels, spoken to Thomas to discourage his doubt; he steps back to the shape of the chapter, observing that the songs of Elisabeth, Mary and Zacharias are all real poetry spoken under the power of the Holy Spirit and stand as the first New Testament hymns, and that every idea in the Magnificat occurs already in the Old Testament. Barnes draws five lessons from Elisabeth's speech and then turns sharply on an inference drawn from the last of them, that the honour warrants worship of the Virgin and prayer offered to her, which he calls an idolatry as gross as any: it is nowhere commanded in the Bible, worship of any being but God is expressly forbidden, and it is besides absurd to suppose that she could be in all places at once to hear the prayers of thousands.

either; it makes good sense both ways

faith holding out its lap

46.pericope_label: My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour

schools.summary: Gill puts the verb as ascribing greatness rather than conferring it, since God cannot be made greater than he is, and notes that Mary did this not in lip and word only but with the whole soul, speaking throughout in the prophetic style, of things as already done which were then doing or shortly to be done. Calvin takes soul and spirit for two faculties, the one the understanding and the other the seat of the affections, and observes that what stands second here comes first in order, since the will is not set going to praise God unless a rejoicing of spirit goes before it — sadness and anxiety lock up the soul and restrain the tongue from celebrating the goodness of God. He notes why the title Saviour belongs just here: until God has been recognised as a Father the mind is not free for true and full joy, and the Greek word means not that he once delivered but that he is the author of an eternal salvation.

Clarke marks a textual curiosity, that two copies of the Itala and some books mentioned by Origen give the song to Elisabeth instead, and disputes the common claim that this is the first piece of poetry in the New Testament, since the angel's address to Zacharias, his address to the virgin, and Elisabeth's answer are all delivered the same way and all reduce to the hemistich form of Hebrew verse. He says the verb signifies to celebrate with words and extol with praises, which is the only way God can be magnified at all, since nothing can be added to one who is infinite and eternal. Wesley draws the sharpest consequence of the second clause: Mary rejoiced in the hope of salvation through faith in her Son, which is a blessing common to all believers, more than in being his mother after the flesh, which was an honour peculiar to herself.

Ellicott introduces the song as the first of the great canticles Luke records, which since the time of Caesarius of Arles, who first brought them into public worship, have belonged to the hymnal treasures of Western Christendom; he supposes the Virgin either committed the words to writing at the time or remembered them afterwards, and notes that the song is manifestly built on Hannah's, both in its opening words and in much of its substance. On the name Saviour he thinks it was chosen for its meaning, which was the very work she had been told would be her Son's. Robertson reports that Harnack argued the song was Elisabeth's from a few Latin manuscripts, and dismisses it: Mary is correct, and she draws her material from the Old Testament and sings in the noblest strain. He will not press the difference between soul and spirit — Bruce calls them synonyms in parallel clauses, Vincent makes the soul the principle of individuality and the spirit the point of contact between God and man, but it is doubtful whether the threefold division of man is to be insisted on at all — and marks the tone, that Mary is not excited as Elisabeth was but breathes a spirit of composed rapture. Barnes gives the verb's range, to make great and then to extol, and rules that here it means to increase in our estimation.

48.pericope_label: He hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden

schools.summary: Augustine reads the phrase as naming a virtue: O true lowliness, he exclaims, which has borne God to men, given life to mortals and opened the gates of Paradise — the lowliness of Mary was made the heavenly ladder by which God descended upon earth. He glosses regarded as approved, since many seem lowly whose lowliness God does not regard, for if they were truly lowly their spirit would rejoice not in the world but in God.

Gill offers both readings of the low estate: the outward one, that David's family was so reduced that its seat had moved from Jerusalem to Nazareth, and the spiritual one, of the estate into which the fall has brought all mankind. Calvin denies flatly that the word means any quality of mind at all. It does not denote submission or modesty, as he says ignorant men have foolishly imagined, but a mean and despicable condition, so that the sense is: I was unknown and despised, and that did not prevent God from deigning to cast his eyes upon me. This was no cry of pretended humility but the honest statement of a conviction engraven on her mind, since she was of no account in the eyes of the world and her estimate of herself was nothing more. On the last clause he argues from the structure of her own sentence: she makes her happiness consist in nothing whatever but what she acknowledges to have been bestowed on her, so that nothing could be more disrespectful to her than to rob the Son of God of what is his own in order to clothe her with the plunder.

Clarke says God visited her in her humiliation in the most compassionate manner, drawing the reasons of his conduct not from any excellence in her but from his own eternal kindness; and he puts the modern use of the verse as an injury to Mary herself, since this was the character by which alone she wished to be known, and those who address her as Queen of Heaven give her names he thinks her pure soul would abhor.

Barnes draws the general rule out of the particular case: notwithstanding her humble rank and poverty God showed her favour, which teaches that he is no respecter of persons and is not influenced by wealth or honour or office, but seeks the humble and gives his richest blessings to those who feel they need them. He agrees it is right to consider her highly favoured and happy, and denies that this warrants worshipping her, since Abraham was blessed in being the father of the faithful and Paul in being the apostle to the Gentiles, and who would think of praying to Abraham or Paul? Ellicott notices that the noun is the same word she had used of herself when she first consented, and grants that the closing words have been partly instrumental in bringing about their own fulfilment, while asking what a vision of the future they must have implied on the part of a village maiden. Robertson keeps the literal sense — the bride of a carpenter, and yet to be the mother of the Messiah — and notes that Elisabeth had already pronounced one such beatitude.

not a quality of mind at all, but a mean and despicable condition — I was unknown and despised

God no respecter of persons

49.pericope_label: He that is mighty hath done to me great things; his mercy is on them that fear him

schools.summary: Augustine answers the question the clause invites by piling up paradoxes: what great things has he done for you, but that a creature, you gave birth to the Creator, a servant, you brought forth the Lord, and that through you God redeemed the world and restored it to life?

Gill names the great thing more soberly as a new and unheard-of work, that a virgin should conceive and bear a Son who is himself the mighty God. Calvin keeps to reverence rather than either purity or kindness in the word holy: the name of God is called holy because it is entitled to the highest reverence, and whenever it is mentioned it ought at once to remind us of his adorable majesty. He marks a structural break here, since with these words Mary leaves the grace shown in her own person and begins to celebrate the power and judgements and mercy of God in general. On the mercy he takes the clause from the solemn form of the covenant and reads it as the favour God continues to show his own people after their death, loving their children and their children's children; but since not all who descend from Abraham after the flesh are the true children of Abraham, Mary confines the promise to those who truly worship God — which leaves no support for the vain confidence of hypocrites. A universal covenant was made with that posterity, he grants, but as stones moistened by rain do not grow soft, the promised righteousness is kept from unbelievers by their own hardness of heart. To the objection that this makes godliness earn the grace it receives, he answers that the fear itself is part of the mercy.

Clarke draws the movement of the verse: as God fills her with his goodness she empties herself to him in praises, and sinking into her own nothingness confesses that God alone is all in all. He suspects the Greek is translating something else, and that the word Mary actually used was one we sometimes render holy but whose proper meaning is abundant goodness, exuberant kindness — a sense that agrees far better with the clause about mercy that immediately follows.

Barnes takes holy in its strict sense and makes it the highest honour she can render: God is free from sin, injustice and impurity, the name being often put for God himself. He defines the fear by contrast — not what a servant feels toward a cruel master, or a man toward a precipice or the plague, but what a dutiful child feels toward a kind and virtuous father, a fear of injuring his feelings or dishonouring him by our life. Robertson confirms that the word here carries its reverential sense, the meaning of dread belonging to other passages. Ellicott hears the clause opening outward instead: as read by those for whom Luke wrote, the words would almost seem to foreshadow the gospel of the Apostle of the Gentiles, since men who feared God were to be found not only among the children of Abraham but in every nation.
