51.pericope_label: He hath scattered the proud; he hath put down the mighty from their seats

schools.summary: Gill offers three readings of the putting down at once: kings put down in the ordinary course of providence, the mighty angels cast from their seats of bliss for opposing the incarnation, and the monarchies of this world broken by the kingdom of the Messiah, at first as mean as a stone cut out of a mountain. Calvin reads the arm as a contrast with every other aid, so that Mary means God rested satisfied with his own power, employed no companions in the work, and called none to help him. On the scattering he finds a figure from the putting to flight of a defeated enemy, and dwells on the phrase about the imagination of their hearts: their pride being outrageous and their covetousness insatiable, they pile their deliberations into an immense heap and build the tower of Babel, until God, having looked down a while in silent mockery on their splendid preparations, scatters the whole mass, as a building is overturned and its parts flung wide. On the reversal of thrones he uses the verse against a rival account: Mary ascribes to the providence and judgements of God what ungodly men call the game of Fortune. Yet he denies this makes God despotic, tossing men up and down like balls: it is a just government founded on the best reasons, though they escape our notice, and if princes brought a sceptre from the womb and thrones never fell, all acknowledgement of God's providence would disappear.

Clarke reports a graded vocabulary Grotius had observed: God's efficacy is represented by his finger, his great power by his hand, his omnipotence by his arm — the plague of lice being the finger of God, the plagues in general his hand, and the destruction of Pharaoh's host his arm. He takes the verb as scattering abroad, as a whirlwind scatters dust and chaff, and derives the adjective from the words meaning above and I show — men who wish to be noticed before all others and feel a sovereign contempt for everyone else; while they lay their plans and imagine success waiting at their right hand, the whirlwind of God's displeasure blows and they and their machinations are dissipated together. Wesley observes that she speaks prophetically of things as done which God was only about to do.

Barnes marks the widening of the song here: the words have no particular reference to God's mercy toward Mary, since from his goodness to herself she enlarges to his goodness at large — which is the nature of true piety, for it does not terminate in God's mercy toward ourselves. He suspects a particular case behind the general one, since Mary was celebrating God's mercies to her own family and it was natural to recall how Saul was overcome and David taken from the sheepfold to the throne; from which he draws a rule about men raised from humble stations to places of great trust, who if they have right feelings will not despise their former companions. Ellicott lists the candidates for the proud without choosing: the potentates of the world she lived in, Herod and the Emperor of Rome; the men of Jerusalem who despised Galilee; those of the other Galilean towns who despised Nazareth; or, less probably, those of Nazareth itself who despised the carpenter and his betrothed. Robertson renders the opening made might, a Hebrew conception, and notes six aorists in this one sentence, none answering to our English idiom; he traces the noun for the mighty to the word that gives us dynasty.

outliers.note: sets the doctrine of providence directly against the idea of Fortune, while denying that it makes God despotic, since the reversals are a just government founded on reasons that escape our notice

who the proud are
providence against the game of Fortune

53.pericope_label: He hath filled the hungry with good things; he hath holpen his servant Israel

schools.summary: Gill names the hungry as those who longed for the Messiah's coming — Simeon, Anna, and all who looked for redemption in Israel — and answers the question who Israel is by saying it is not the natural posterity of Jacob but the elect among them, since all were not Israel who were of Israel, and not those only but the chosen among the Gentiles. Calvin calls the verb rendered holpen an elegant metaphor of taking a falling person by the hand, and insists the state of the nation warranted it: the public instruction retained almost nothing pure, the government of the Church was in the greatest confusion and breathed nothing but shocking barbarity, the order of civil society no longer subsisted, and the people were torn like wild beasts by the Romans and by Herod — so that the restoration was the more glorious for being one which so desperate a case gave no ground to expect. He explains the last clause as the reason for the whole: God lifted up the fallen nation to give an illustration of his mercy, and Mary says he remembered that mercy because he might have seemed in some sort to have forgotten it while he allowed his people to be so fearfully afflicted. Since the human mind forms no conception of the divine mercy except as it is declared in the word, she directs her attention and ours to the promises — which is why Calvin infers that she was unusually well acquainted with Scripture, the expectation of a Messiah being general in that age while few had so pure a knowledge.

Clarke pictures God daily feeding multitudes at his gates, poor and rich alike dependent on him: the poor man comes through a sense of want and is fed, the rich man through the lust of gain, to get more added to his abundance, and is sent away empty — not merely given nothing more, but often deprived of what he had. He narrows the falling to a single house, since the family of David was ready to fall and rise no more, and Jesus, born of the last branch of the regal line, revived it and restored the dominion; and he takes the mercy to be the covenant made with Abraham, in which salvation was promised to all the nations of the earth.

Barnes says the poor come that their daily wants may be supplied, the rich with lofty hearts and insatiable desires that their riches may be increased — better to be poor and go to God for daily bread than rich and forget our dependence on him; and he makes the image of the verb more precise, of taking hold of one to help him up when he is in danger of falling. Ellicott hears the beatitudes of the Sermon on the Plain anticipated here, with both a literal and a spiritual fulfilment: those who trusted in earthly riches and those who gloried in a fancied spiritual wealth were alike sent empty away, while the hungry who craved a higher blessedness were filled. He hears the hymn turn outward at this point, the whole soul of the maiden of Nazareth being now with her people, and adds a note on the date: a hope of restoration voiced as already realised suggests an early hymn, since by the time Luke wrote it was the rejection of Israel that occupied men's minds. Robertson defines the verb as laying hold of a thing with a view to help or succour, and notes that the noun beside it means servant here rather than son or child.

outliers.note: argues from the hymn's confidence about Israel's restoration that it must be early, since by the time Luke wrote it was the rejection of Israel that filled men's minds

how far the nation had fallen
the date the hymn implies

55.pericope_label: As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever

schools.summary: Gill traces the speaking to three fathers in turn — to David, of whose family Mary was, to Jacob, of whose stock she was, and to Isaac, in whom the seed was to be called — and notes that three months was the term the Jewish doctors laid down for determining whether a woman was with child, so that by the end of it Mary had full satisfaction about the sign the angel had given her. Calvin agrees that the clause about the fathers is to be read as a parenthesis, but denies that the connection is as close as some make it: Mary is not merely identifying the fathers to whom God spoke, but extending the power and the result of the promises to all Abraham's posterity, so long as they are his true seed. The covenant in view here was made in a peculiar manner with Abraham and his descendants, whereas the promises given earlier to Adam and to Noah looked indiscriminately to all nations; and since many of Abraham's children after the flesh have been cut off by unbelief, we who were strangers are admitted by faith and reckoned his true seed. On the length of the visit he thinks Mary had no other reason for staying so long than to enjoy that exhibition of divine grace which the angel had named for the confirming of her faith, and adds what the whole narrative is for: the birth of John was distinguished by various miracles which gave reason to expect something great in the child.

Wesley says in four words that the seed meant is the spiritual seed, all true believers, and notes that Mary returned to her own house, and thence soon after to Bethlehem. Clarke observes that on some reckonings the departure came only a few days before the birth of John, since nine months had by then elapsed since Elisabeth conceived.

Ellicott sets out a difficulty the English hides: as the sentence stands in our version the words about Abraham and his seed look like an apposition explaining our forefathers, whereas in the Greek they stand in a different connection and belong to what went before, so that the sense runs, to remember his mercy — as he spake to our forefathers — to Abraham and to his seed for ever. On the visit he feels the pull of both possibilities, since the time is brought so close to the birth that we might well think the Virgin waited for it, and yet the next verse seems almost to imply that she had already gone. Barnes takes the promise particularly referred to as the one now about to be fulfilled concerning the Messiah, while allowing that all the other mercies conferred on the children of Israel are included with it, and reads the closing words for ever back into the previous verse.

57.pericope_label: Elisabeth's full time came, and her neighbours rejoiced with her

schools.summary: Gill counts the months out: the nine were now complete, since the angel came to Mary in the sixth month of Elisabeth's pregnancy and Mary stayed about three, and he supposes she had left in order to avoid the company that would gather at the delivery. He places that company in and about Hebron, whether of the house of Aaron or of the tribe of Judah, to both of which Elisabeth was related. Calvin leaves open whether the neighbours measured the kindness simply by her having a child at all, or whether they had already heard that an angel appeared to Zacharias; on either view it was no ordinary favour that a barren woman at a very advanced age should bring forth out of the course of nature. He notes what the eighth day then made of the occasion, since people assemble from a sense of duty or from courtesy and God takes the opportunity to make them witnesses and spectators of his power; and from the size of the gathering he infers a practice — that though children were circumcised at home, it was not done without collecting a numerous assembly, and with good reason, since this was a common sacrament of the church and not properly administered in a private manner.

Henry draws a lesson from there being a term at all: though the child was conceived by miracle he continued in the womb according to the ordinary course of nature, as our Saviour did after him, so promised mercies are to be expected when the full time is come, and not before. Following Lightfoot he distinguishes the company, the priests of Aaron's family in the city being the kindred and the children of Judah in the fields and villages round about being the neighbours; and he finds two regards in the scene at once — a pious regard to God, since they acknowledged that the Lord had magnified his mercy, and a friendly regard to Elisabeth, since when she rejoiced they rejoiced with her.

Clarke reports the alternative reckoning, that the three months of the visit preceded the birth and completed the term. He then turns the neighbours' joy into three obligations: a duty of humanity, since we are members of one another and he who rejoices in his neighbour's prosperity increases his neighbour's happiness and gets an addition to his own; a duty of charity, to be performed with sincerity, since in the polite world no duty is better fulfilled in word while sincerity is utterly banished and both parties know the compliments mean nothing, and the man who does not take a sincere part in his neighbour's prosperity will soon feel ample punishment in jealousy and envy; and a duty of religion, since these neighbours saw that God had magnified his mercy and acknowledged his hand in the work.

Ellicott prefers kindred to cousins as covering a wider range of relations than our own word does, and thinks the wording implies they had heard something of the vision in the Temple and of what was foretold of the child's greatness; he notices too that the phrase for what God had done uses the verb that opens the Magnificat, so the sentence may be read as an echo of it. Robertson marks the same verb and adds that the imperfect pictures a continual joy, its prefix carrying the sense of rejoicing together.

59.pericope_label: On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and called him Zacharias

schools.summary: Chrysostom sets the rite in its whole history: circumcision was first delivered to Abraham as a mark of distinction, that the patriarch's race might be preserved in unmixed purity and so be able to obtain the promises; but now that the promise of the covenant is fulfilled the sign attached to it is removed, so that through Christ circumcision ceased and baptism came in its place — though it was right that John should first be circumcised. He offers two reasons why the eighth day was appointed in mercy: because in its most tender years a child more easily bears the cutting of the flesh, and because the very operation reminds us that the thing was done for a sign. On the naming he explains the order: after the circumcision the name was conferred, because we must first receive the seal of the Lord and then the name of man.

Gill notes that the eighth day was the time fixed by the ordinance, though it was not always kept and circumcision was sometimes deferred. Calvin takes the occasion for a short history of naming. Names were originally given either from some occurrence or by prophetic inspiration, to point out some secret work of God; but after a long period, when there was such a profusion of them that it became inconvenient to form new ones every day, people contented themselves with the old received names and called their children after their ancestors — so that before the father of John there had been many a Zacharias. Use and wont, he adds drily, is generally taken for law, and that is why these people argued that the prevailing custom ought to be followed here. He will not pretend there is any sacredness in a name, and yet holds that believers ought in this matter to make a godly and profitable selection, giving their children such names as may serve to instruct and admonish them.

Clarke draws a different consequence from the same delay: had circumcision been essential to an infant's salvation God would not have ordered it deferred to the eighth day, since in every country multitudes die before that age — and baptism, which is generally allowed to have been substituted for it, is no more necessary to an infant's salvation than circumcision was, both being signs of the covenant, and neither on that account to be neglected. He agrees that among the Jews the name was given at the circumcision and that the eldest son ordinarily received his father's.

Ellicott compares the occasion to the baptism of infants among Christians, a day when relatives were invited as witnesses and which was commonly followed by a feast, and explains how the company came to be naming the child at all: the choice commonly rested with the father, but the kinsfolk seem to have assumed that in his dumbness the duty had devolved on them, and by a custom not uncommon they showed their respect for him by choosing his name. He adds what a name was for, that it should bear witness to the prayers of the parents and to the child's own relation to the God of his fathers. Barnes says the same about the eldest son receiving the father's name; Robertson catches the tense, which is conative — they were trying to call him so.

60.pericope_label: His name is John; and his mouth was opened immediately

schools.summary: Gill checks a version against the fact, since the Persic makes the relatives say there was no one of this name in Israel, which cannot be true, Jochanan being a very common name though not in this family. Calvin thinks it likely that a man who had seen what his slowness to believe had cost him would take care to inform his wife of what the angel enjoined, since otherwise he would not have obeyed the command at all; and he sees a design in the timing of the cure, the benefit having been delayed to that day on purpose, to fix the eyes of men on the child. Zacharias spoke not only to testify gratitude but to let his neighbours know why the punishment had fallen on him — not ashamed to unite his own dishonour with the praises of the divine glory, so that it became universally known that this birth was no accidental or ordinary event.

Clarke finds the whole household named significantly: Zachariah is the memorial of Jehovah, Elisabeth the rest of my strong God, and John, which he would always write Jehochanan, the grace or mercy of Jehovah — a name given because the child was to go before and proclaim the God of all grace. He explains that the genealogical tables were carefully preserved in each family for the sake of distinguishing inheritances, so that a name never before used in any branch would naturally be resisted; and he reports a friend's proposal to redistribute the verses, on the ground that a man whose mouth was not opened until after the naming could not have asked for the tablet, rejecting it since neither the words of the Greek nor their construction will bear it, though he does move the clause about their marvelling forward, holding that the people wondered not at the choice of name but at the speech restored that instant. Wesley prefers the shorter explanation of the mother's knowledge, that she spoke by revelation or a particular impulse from God.

Barnes supposes Zacharias had told his wife by writing, and explains that the Jewish tribes and families were kept distinct, so that to avoid confusion in the genealogical tables they probably used only those names found among their ancestors, with the added motive of respect for honoured parents. Ellicott adds that what follows shows the writing-tablet had been in frequent use, and draws an inference of another kind from the absence of the name: it probably shows that Zacharias did not belong to the circle related to the Sadducean high priests, among whom the name does appear some thirty years later. He takes it as almost certain that Zacharias had lost hearing as well as speech, describes the tablets in common use throughout the Roman empire as wooden and covered with a thin coat of wax, written on with the sharp point that survives in our word style, and hears something emphatic in the present tense of the answer — his name is John — since this was not a question open for discussion. Robertson notes the imperfect tense of the signs, the repeated action usual in making them, and adds that the same word for tablet was used of a physician's note-book.

65.pericope_label: Fear came on all; and they said, What manner of child shall this be!

schools.summary: Gill takes the fear for the fear of God, an awful reverence of the divine majesty, since they perceived the hand of God was in these things. Calvin uses the same fear to say what miracles are for: it proceeded from a feeling of the divine power, and the works of God ought to be contemplated with such reverence as to affect our minds in earnest; he does not amuse us with miracles as with a pastime, but arouses the senses of men which he sees to be stupefied and asleep. Yet many derived no lasting advantage from the impression, since when John began to exercise his office there were few who remembered what wonders had attended his birth — which is why Calvin holds the report was spread abroad not merely for the sake of those who heard it but to establish the certainty of the miracle in all ages. He sees in the failure a general mirror of human ingratitude: while trifling and frivolous occurrences remain firmly in our minds, the things which ought to produce a constant recollection of God's favours fade at once. He is careful not to overstate it, since Luke is not speaking of stupid men or open despisers.

Clarke locates the impression precisely: the inhabitants of Hebron and its environs, who knew the circumstances of Zacharias and Elisabeth, perceived that God had visited them in a remarkable manner, and this begot a more than ordinary reverence — so that, he adds, the salvation of one often becomes an instrument of good to the souls of many. He thinks the people of that hill country an open and honest-hearted sort, readier than townspeople to acknowledge the interposition of God, and draws the inference the neighbours drew, that after so many extraordinary things God had surely designed the child for some extraordinary purpose. Wesley glosses the hand of the Lord as the peculiar power and blessing of God.

Robertson says the fear is not terror but religious awe at contact with the supernatural, the same word used of Zacharias in the temple, and notes that the verb for the spreading of the news is an imperfect describing continuous talk passing back and forth among the people; he treats the clause about the hand as Luke's own explanation added to the supernatural events, observing that the phrase occurs only in his writings. Barnes agrees that the word denotes reverence and glosses the hand as aid, protection and favour, since we stretch out the hand to help those we wish to assist. Ellicott describes the district as the mountain plateau south of Jerusalem, reaching its highest point at Hebron, and corrects the common mistranslation of the question: not what kind of child this should be, but what the child would grow to. He notes that some good manuscripts supply a conjunction before the last clause, making the hand of the Lord the reason for the question, and explains the idiom — the hand standing for what we more commonly call the guidance or providence of God, one of those vivid expressions the Hebrews could use more boldly than other nations precisely because they had clearer thoughts of God as not made after the similitude of men.

outliers.note: reads the neighbours' short memory as a mirror of human ingratitude, and argues that the report was spread abroad less for their sake than to establish the miracle's certainty in every later age

67.pericope_label: Zacharias was filled with the Holy Ghost, and prophesied

schools.summary: Gill notes that his wife had been so filled before him. Calvin explains what the filling adds to a man who already had the Spirit: the servants of God receive more abundantly a grace of which at other times they were not destitute, and so the Spirit is said to be given to the prophets — not that they otherwise wanted it, but that its power was more fully exerted in them when the hand of God brought them into public view for the discharge of their office. He notes how closely Luke joins the two clauses, which implies that inspiration rested on Zacharias in an extraordinary measure, so that all he uttered was heavenly instruction; Paul likewise couples prophecy with the Spirit, teaching us that to despise instruction is to quench the Spirit's light. And it was a remarkable instance of God's goodness that the man not only recovered the speech he had lacked for nine months but had his tongue made the organ of the Holy Ghost.

Henry says God not only forgave the unbelief, which was signified by discharging him from its punishment, but filled him with the Spirit and put this honour on him, as a specimen of the abounding of grace toward believers. He is struck by what the song leaves out: nothing is said of the private concerns of his own family, of the reproach rolled away from it or the reputation put on it, though no doubt he found a time to give thanks for that with his household; here he is wholly taken up with the kingdom of the Messiah and the public blessings to be brought in by it, since he could have had little pleasure in the fruitfulness of his own vine had he not foreseen the good of Jerusalem and peace upon Israel. Henry observes too that Old Testament prophecy is often expressed in praises and new songs, and that the beginning of New Testament prophecy takes the same form; and he asks why a man speaking of a redemption for the world should call God the Lord God of Israel, answering that to Israel the prophecies and promises and types of that redemption had hitherto been given.

Clarke takes the word prophesy in what he calls its proper acceptation, of predicting or foretelling future events, since Zacharias speaks not only of what God had done but of what he was about to do in order to save a lost world. Wesley makes the same point about proportion from the other end, that Zacharias speaks of Christ chiefly and of his own son only, as it were, incidentally.

Ellicott prefers the wider sense of an inspired utterance of praise, and offers an account of the hymn's origin: it appears as the report, written probably by Zacharias himself, of the praises uttered in the first moments of his recovered speech, so that we may think of it as expressing the pent-up thoughts of the months of silence — the fire had long been kindling, and at last he spake with his tongue. Barnes resolves the difference by allowing the word all three senses at once, to foretell, to celebrate the praises of God, and to teach or preach, and observing that this song partakes of all three. Robertson notes that nearly every phrase in it comes from the Psalms and the Prophets, and that Zacharias, like Mary, had caught the Messianic message in its highest meaning.

68.pericope_label: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who hath raised up an horn of salvation

schools.summary: Chrysostom takes the horn simply for power, glory and honour, drawn metaphorically from the brute creatures, to whom God has given horns for defence and for ornament.

Gill begins with the form of words, a blessing probably in use ever since Israel became a body politic, and is careful about what blessing God can mean: not invoking a blessing on him, since there is none greater of whom to ask one, nor conferring one, but praising and glorifying him. Calvin asks why the God whose government the whole world is subject to should be named the God of Israel, and answers that the Redeemer had been promised to the seed of Abraham in a peculiar manner; the verb that follows carries an implied contrast, since the face of God had for a time been turned from those unhappy children, sunk so deep in calamity that no one supposed his eye was on them. He holds that the two prepositions in the verse, spelled the same, do not mean the same, and draws a further consequence from the redemption: since those whom God redeems must be prisoners and this redemption is spiritual, even the holy fathers were freed from the yoke of sin only through the grace of Christ, and to the objection that believers who died earlier must then have been slaves all their lifetime he answers that the power and efficacy of that one redemption have been the same in all ages. On the horn he reads it as saving power: when the throne of David was cast down and the people scattered, the hope of salvation had to all appearance perished, and Zacharias alludes to those predictions which promise a sudden revival when affairs have become desperate — a horn bringing salvation to believers and terror to the ungodly.

Clarke takes the word for redemption in its strict sense of ransoming a captive from the enemy by paying a price, and quotes Josephus on Herod paying three hundred talents for his brother. On the horn he prefers the altar, adding that Christ is a new altar to which whoever flees will find refuge, and canvasses others besides: that the Chaldee paraphrast sometimes renders the word kingdom, and that a horn filled with fruits was the old emblem of abundance. Wesley reads the figure for honour, plenty and strength together, and the whole phrase as meaning a glorious and mighty Saviour.

Ellicott makes the point about the visitation with a date attached: the four centuries since the last of the prophets are thought of as a time when the face of the Lord was turned away, and now he looks on his people again — not to visit them for their offences, but to deliver. He observes how large an element the thought of deliverance through a ransom was in the Messianic expectation of the time, and notes that the past tense is prophetic foresight seeing the end of what had only begun, the next verse making clear that Zacharias looked for the redemption not through his own child but through the Son of Mary. Barnes renders the second verb literally, that God has made a ransom for his people: a ransom was the price paid to deliver a captive taken in war, and the death of Jesus in the place of sinners is what God accepts instead of their eternal sufferings — not itself a punishment, since punishment supposes personal crime, but an equivalent showing the same hatred of sin. On the horn he suggests the image may come from the Jewish altar, at each of whose corners was a projection called a horn which a man in danger might lay hold of. Robertson traces the verb for visiting from looking upon to visiting in order to give aid.

70.pericope_label: As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, that we should be saved from our enemies

schools.summary: Gill finds in the clause both the veracity of God in his promises and the earliness of the intimations he gave about the Messiah, and lists the enemies as sin, Satan, the world, the law as the killing letter, and death as the last enemy to be destroyed. Calvin explains why the prophets are summoned at this point: so that the salvation brought by Christ should not be thought doubtful on the score of novelty. They were raised up at different times and yet teach with one consent that salvation is to be expected from Christ alone, and when he comes forth adorned with the testimonies of all of them our faith rests on a truly solid foundation; Zacharias calls them holy to secure greater authority for their words, since these were not ordinary witnesses but of the first rank. He then states a rule for reading them: it is enough that they all uniformly make the hope of the people rest entirely on that covenant which was founded on Christ, and whoever neglects the signature of the divine covenant will never understand anything in the prophets at all. On the enemies he says Zacharias was well aware that the principal war of the church of God is not with flesh and blood but with Satan and all his armament, and though the Church is attacked by outward foes too, the kingdom of Christ being spiritual, the discourse relates chiefly to the prince of this world. He draws two consequences: that men out of Christ lie prostrate under the tyranny of the devil, and that so long as the Church continues her pilgrimage she lives among her foes.

Clarke argues from the inspiration itself that the salvation must be spiritual, and names Satan, death and sin, of which sin is the most dangerous and properly the only enemy we have to fear, since Satan is outside us and can have no power over us except what he gets through sin, while death is only in our flesh and will be destroyed on the morning of the resurrection. Wesley takes the opposite line to Barnes on the antiquity of the prophets, holding in a sentence that there were prophets from the very beginning.

Barnes lists the most striking of the prophets — Jacob, Moses, Isaiah — and enters one caution, that the phrase since the world began is not to be taken literally, for there were no prophets immediately after the creation; on the enemies he names man's sins, his carnal propensities and lusts, and the great adversary with his angels. Ellicott stands between Barnes and Wesley, thinking the words more than a lofty paraphrase for of old time and hearing in them a reference to the first promise in Genesis as well as to Abraham, who is the earliest man actually called a prophet. On the enemies he alone takes them as the men present to the speaker's own thoughts — the Roman conquerors of Judaea, with the Idumaean house of Herod perhaps among those who hate. Robertson would simply render the phrase from of old.

72.pericope_label: To remember his holy covenant, the oath which he sware to our father Abraham

schools.summary: Gill takes the mercy promised to be salvation by Christ, and notes that the fathers under the Old Testament were saved by the same grace, his blood having been shed for the remission of sins that were past; on the oath he recalls that God swore by himself, because he could swear by no greater, that in blessing he would bless Abraham. Calvin sets out the order in which the thing happened and insists the order matters. First, God was moved by pure mercy to make a covenant with the fathers. Second, he linked the salvation of men to his own word, so that it depends on it. Third, he exhibited every blessing in Christ, so as to ratify all his promises, whose truth is only confirmed to us when we see them fulfilled in him: forgiveness is promised in the covenant, but it is in the blood of Christ; righteousness is promised, but offered through his atonement; life is promised, but must be sought only in his death and resurrection. He explains the word remember in the same way, since there might well be some appearance of forgetfulness during that long delay in which God let his people languish under very heavy calamities. That the promise reaches backward as well as forward is his next point: Zacharias speaks of a mercy shown in his own generation as extending to fathers already dead, from which it follows that the grace and power of Christ are not confined within the narrow limits of this fading life. On the oath he explains why one is mentioned at all — it expresses more fully the firmness and sacredness of God's truth, since he deigns to employ his own name to support our weakness, and if his bare promises do not satisfy us we are chargeable with heinous ingratitude and with insult to his holy name.

Ellicott finds a hidden signature in the verse: after the manner of the ancient prophets it plays on three names at once, performing mercy alluding to John, which means the Lord be merciful; remembering his holy covenant to Zacharias, whom Jehovah remembers; and the oath of the next verse to Elisabeth, the oath of my God — a play obvious in the Aramaic of the hymn, which survives only in its Greek version. He takes the covenant to be the one made with Abraham, and observes that in going back to it as the starting point of the new covenant in Christ, Zacharias anticipates Paul's teaching in Galatians; he notes too that the noun for oath stands in apposition to the covenant of the previous verse. Barnes uses the occasion for a definition: covenant among men implies equality between the parties, freedom from constraint, and freedom to decline, and such a transaction can never take place between man and God, since man may not refuse what God proposes and is already bound to do all that God commands — so in Scripture the word means sometimes a command, sometimes a promise, sometimes a law, and sometimes the way in which God dispenses mercy. Robertson notes the attraction by which the antecedent has been drawn into the case of the relative, and adds that the oppression of the Gentiles seems to have been in the speaker's mind, though it is uncertain how clearly he grasped the idea of a spiritual Israel.

outliers.note: detects a prophetic play on the names of Zacharias, Elisabeth and John within these two verses, visible in the Aramaic beneath the Greek

74.pericope_label: That we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness all our days

schools.summary: Chrysostom points out that the verse claims two things not easily found together: many escape danger but fail of a glorious life, like criminals discharged from prison by the king's mercy, while others reap glory but must encounter dangers for its sake, as soldiers embrace an honourable life and are often in the greatest peril. The horn brings both at once. On the next verse he divides the duty — holiness a proper observance of what we owe God, righteousness of what we owe men — and adds the point of the phrase that follows: Zacharias does not say before men, as of hypocrites desirous to please men, but before God; and not once or for a time, but all the days of their life. He notes too what kind of service is meant: not in the flesh with the blood of victims, but in the spirit with good works.

Gill makes the same contrast: not mere outward rites and ceremonies but the principles of righteousness and true holiness in which the new man is created. Calvin fixes on the purpose clause: the redeemed were to consecrate themselves entirely to the Author of their salvation, for as the efficient cause of salvation was the undeserved goodness of God, its final cause is that by a holy life men should glorify his name. We are redeemed at a great price, he says, not to serve the lusts of the flesh but that Christ may reign in us. On the words without fear he holds that we cannot worship God properly without composure of mind: men who are ill at ease, struggling over whether God is favourable or hostile and whether he accepts or rejects their services, may labour anxiously in worship but will never sincerely obey, since alarm and dread make them turn from him with horror. No sacrifice is acceptable which is not offered willingly and with a cheerful heart, so men must obtain peace of conscience before they can truly worship.

Clarke gathers the passage into a summary of what salvation consists in: deliverance from our enemies, so that sin has neither dominion nor existence in us; the worship of God; holiness, an inward conformity to the mind of Christ, and righteousness, a full outward conformity to the precepts of the gospel; all done before God, under the continual support of his grace; and a blessedness continuing as long as we exist. What a pity, he adds, to have lived so long without God in the world, when so much happiness and glory are to be enjoyed in union with him. Wesley calls the fear slavish fear, and hears in the verse the substance of the great promise — that we shall be always holy and always happy, joyfully serving God in every thought, word and work.

Ellicott finds the Greek plainer than the English that this was the end to which the covenant and the oath had been pointing all along, the service meant being worship as well as obedience; and he notes again that the shape of the hope suggests an early date, since by the time Luke wrote there was no prospect of the Jews being delivered from earthly enemies — what was transitory in the hymn had vanished, and the words had gained the permanent sense they keep in the worship of the Church. On the two nouns he says holiness has special reference to man's relations with God and justice to those that connect him with his fellow men, though the words overlap. Barnes lists what the fear would be of: death, spiritual enemies, external foes. Robertson observes that the verb for serving originally meant service for hire.

outliers.note: makes peace of conscience a precondition of worship rather than its reward, holding that a man uncertain whether God accepts him may labour anxiously but will never sincerely obey

76.pericope_label: Thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest, to give knowledge of salvation

schools.summary: Gill notes that the words are spoken for the sake of those present rather than the infant, and presses the title: the Highest here is the Lord Jesus, whose forerunner John was, which Gill takes as proof that Christ is the most high God. He rules out the salvation the nation was hoping for, since John gave no intimation of deliverance from the Roman yoke, and adds that the knowledge meant is not merely notional but experimental, and is a gift rather than something acquired by industry. Calvin explains the licence of addressing a week-old child: Zacharias observes no prophetical endowments in an infant of eight days, but turns his eyes to the purpose of God and speaks of it as already settled, since a secret calling had taken place and it only remained that its nature be made known to men. On the second verse he treats the clause as the principal subject of the gospel: since we are by nature children of wrath and are chargeable with unrighteousness, there is no provision for escaping eternal death but God reconciling us to himself and not imputing our trespasses. True righteousness, he concludes, is nothing else than the imputation of righteousness, when God out of free grace acquits us from guilt — and since Zacharias is speaking not of strangers to the covenant but of the people of God, believers stand righteous before him by imputation to the very end.

Clarke works through the prediction in parts, taking it to proclaim the dignity, the employment, the doctrine and the success of the son. Prophet, he says, has two acceptations — one who foretells future events, and a teacher of men in the things of God — and John was both; even his name was a standing prediction of the salvation of God, and he had the honour of being the last and clearest prophet of the old covenant and the first of the new. As to the employment, he was to be the immediate forerunner of Christ, none being capable of succeeding him in that ministry but Christ himself. What he was to teach Clarke calls the science of salvation: men are ignorant and must be instructed, and the human sciences, profitable as they may be in earthly matters, cannot profit the soul — the science which teaches God must come from God. Wesley takes the immediate sense to be that John was to preach salvation by the remission of sins.

Ellicott notes the recurrence of the divine name that had appeared earlier in the chapter, and hears in the verse an echo of two prophecies at once, the going before Jehovah of Malachi and the preparing of the way from Isaiah. On the aim of the mission he says men had lost sight of the true nature of salvation, being wrapt in dreams of deliverance from outward enemies, and needed teaching that it consisted in forgiveness for past sins and power to overcome sin in future; he notes too that these are historically the first words about the remission of sins in the Gospel records, and sets them beside our Lord's words at the Last Supper, since the two ministries, different as they were in outward form, agreed in this. Barnes puts it more briefly: a prophet is one appointed by God to declare his will, and to go before a man's face is simply to go immediately before him. Robertson observes that the word prophet is applied directly to the child, whom Jesus would afterwards call more than a prophet.

outliers.note: marks this as the first utterance in the Gospel records of the phrase remission of sins, and reads it as the key-note of a work running from the Baptist to the Last Supper

78.pericope_label: The dayspring from on high hath visited us, to give light to them that sit in darkness

schools.summary: Gill spells out how far back the mercy reaches: it moved God to enter into covenant with his Son, to set him forth in the eternal purposes and to send him in the fulness of time; and whatever the pardon of our sins cost God and Christ, it is all free grace to us. He identifies those in darkness as God's elect among the Jews, in the darkness not only of an unregenerate state but of the legal dispensation, having lost the knowledge of God's righteousness under blind guides. Calvin says Zacharias was not satisfied with calling this the salvation brought by Christ, but used more emphatic language and traced it to the very bowels of God; he reads the next word as a metaphor of the great mercy of God making the day to dawn, and hears behind it Malachi's prediction, where Christ is called the Sun of Righteousness and is said to arise with healing in his wings. On the last verse he raises the obvious objection — how could Israelites be said to sit in darkness, when the Lord always shone on their hearts by faith? — and answers that the godly under the law were surrounded on every side by the darkness of death and saw at a distance, in the coming of Christ, the light that cheered them and kept them from being overwhelmed. He adds that peace here must carry the full Hebrew sense of every kind of prosperity, so that we may not seek the smallest portion of happiness anywhere but in Christ.

Ellicott renders the first phrase literally as the bowels of mercy of our God, and explains that this was how the Jews spoke of what we should call the heart of God; he insists too on the force of the preposition, since the pity that moved that heart is thought of not as the instrument through which but as that on account of which the Baptist's work was to be done. On the dayspring he thinks the English word catches the Greek beautifully, the dawn being seen in the east rising upward and breaking through the darkness; but the same word had acquired a distinctly Messianic association through its use in the Septuagint for the Branch, that which springs upward, so that here a name which had become Messianic is taken in its primary sense and turned into a parable. He hears an echo of Isaiah in the last verse and carries the image further, the sunrise lighting the path of men who had sat all night in a dark ravine and whose feet are now guided into the way of peace — a word which with the Hebrews always included every form of blessedness. Barnes takes the dayspring for the morning light, the aurora, the rising of the sun, and explains the qualifier — it is the dayspring from on high because the light of the gospel shines out from heaven; he then turns the closing verse into a picture of travellers overtaken by night, waiting patiently for the morning that they may see which way to go. Robertson gives the same literal rendering of the first phrase, notes the margin's hearts of mercy, agrees that the word for dayspring can be used of a sprouting plant but says that does not suit the context, and adds a sober aside on the last clause: we are still on that road, though so many stumble for lack of light, men and nations alike.

80.pericope_label: The child grew, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel

schools.summary: Gill has the child growing in stature of body while increasing in wisdom and knowledge and in fortitude of soul, and closes by identifying him simply as John, the son of Zacharias and Elisabeth.

Clarke has him increasing in stature and bodily vigour while his understanding was divinely illuminated and confirmed in the truths of God, adds the neighbourhood of Nazareth to the places named, and takes the last phrase of his thirtieth year, before which the law did not permit a man to enter the public ministry.

Barnes reads the second clause as courage, understanding and purposes of good, all fitting him for his future work, and pauses over the English verb, which means simply to increase and comes from an old Saxon word; he places the child in Hebron and the hill country where his father had lived, dwelling in obscurity and unknown publicly to the people, and reads the last phrase as the entry on the ministry recorded by Matthew. Ellicott admits at once that we have no materials for filling up the outline, and then sets down what may fairly be surmised: the usual Jewish education, the observance of the Nazarite vow, the death of his parents while he was still comparatively young, an early retirement to the deserts round the western shores of the Dead Sea, study and meditation given to the Law and the Prophets, a steadfast waiting for the consolation of Israel, and possible intercourse with the Essenes of that region or with hermit-teachers like Banus, the master of Josephus. This much is probable, he says, and we cannot say more; but whatever the surroundings, the man entered on his work in a spirit intensely personal and original. Robertson notes that both Greek verbs are imperfects, so that the sentence describes a child who kept on growing rather than one who had arrived, that the noun for the showing occurs here alone in the New Testament though found in Plutarch and Polybius, and that the related verb carries a sacrificial sense. He ends on the two childhoods the chapter has set side by side: the boy may well have gone up to the passover and even seen the boy Jesus there without knowing he was to be the Messiah, so that these two children of destiny grew on with the years, the one in the desert hills near Hebron after his parents had died, the other the young carpenter up in Nazareth, each waiting for his own showing unto Israel.

outliers.note: marks the boundary between conjecture and evidence for the Baptist's hidden years, listing what may fairly be surmised and refusing to go beyond it
